newsitem.title: USA: U.S., EU meat talks extended as key issues remain.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU meat talks extended as key issues remain.

text.p: European officals trying to settle a nasty fight with the United States over meat and poultry imports will meet on Friday in hopes that a last-ditch effort would avert a trade war.

"I am hopeful that by staying on here another day, we can go back to Europe and have this question settled," said Lars Hoelgaard, the senior EU negotiator at ongoing talks between Brussels and Washington on meat inspection regulations.

Hoelgaard and the head U.S. negotiator, Paul Drazek, both agreed in separate press briefings that after more than 16 hours of negotiators over the past three days, progress had been made, but that a key sticking point remained unresolved.
"It would be safe to say that the odds have improved" towards reaching an agreement," Drazek said.
How U.S. poultry plants decontaminate chicken and turkey carcasses has become what appears to be the biggest remaining hurdle in reaching an agreement in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks.
A deal would allow each side to accept meat and poultry from the other even if safety inspection methods differ.
The failure to reach an agreement last week sparked trans-Atlantic moves that could disrupt the flow of hundreds of millions of dollars worth of trade.

The European Union on April 1 imposed new rules that could halt up to $50 million worth of poultry to the United States, and in return, the United States announced new regulations that come April 15, could stop some $300 million worth of European meat products from entering the country.

U.S. and EU officials have been meeting all week to work out a deal before April 15. EU officials had been set to leave Washington late this afternoon, but at the last minute, with their bags already packed, they cancelled their flights and said they would stay for one more day of talks.

Officials said they had settled conflicts over certain red meat issues, and announced that an agreement had been reached which would enable some $30 million worth of U.S. dairy product exports to continue to flow to the EU.
But the differences in the U.S. and EU's poultry processing methods were proving the hardest obstacles to overcome -- specifically the decontamination issue.

The U.S. poultry industry dips or sprays carcasses with a chlorine solution to kill bacteria. The EU does not like the decontamination method in general, and especially using chlorine, which it claims can cause cancer.

On Thursday, the EU offered to do a scientific review of the use of decontamination in poultry plants, but said the plan would only study the use of lactic acid and TSP in the decontamination process, and not of chlorine.
The U.S. industry contends using TSP -- trisodium phosphate -- would cost 10 times more than chlorine and said that lactic acid is not a commonly used substance in America.

U.S. officials said the EU's exclusion of chlorine in their plan is a big concern, but said Washington is seriously studying the proposal. Officials said they wanted to get feedback from the poultry industry, which has already expressed reservations about the proposal.
U.S. meat and poultry industry officials have supported the administration's hardline approach in this latest round of negotiations in the years-old dispute.
The hope has been that pushing the issue to the point of a major trade disruption would give negotiators more cause to settle the issue.

"Being faced with certain repercussions always brings a little clarity of focus to the negotiation process and adds incentive on both sides to work out a deal," said an official with the National Cattlemen's Beef Association.
